sections.title: Prevalence, screening and metabolic associations
sections.contentHtml:
17–46%Western adults
7%Lean individuals
~50%Diagnosed late
12–22%Chronic liver disease patients
  • Screen patients with insulin resistance or metabolic risk factors for NAFLD.
  • Evaluate steatosis for secondary causes, alcohol intake and coexisting chronic liver disease.
  • Assess metabolic syndrome features independent of liver-enzyme levels.
  • In NAFLD, diabetes screening is mandatory; in T2DM, look for NAFLD regardless of liver enzymes.
  • Community screening is limited by cost, low predictive value of available tests, biopsy risk and lack of approved specific pharmacotherapy in the source.

sections.title: Diagnosis, biopsy and non-invasive assessment
sections.contentHtml:
1. 1
    Document steatosis: ultrasonography is the preferred first-line imaging test.
  2. 2
    Assess metabolic risk and exclude secondary causes, viral hepatitis and other chronic liver diseases.
  3. 3
    Estimate fibrosis risk using biomarkers/scores and transient elastography.
  4. 4
    Confirm advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis with biopsy when clinically required.
  5. 5
    Use liver biopsy for definitive NASH diagnosis.
  • Fibrosis stage is the most important prognostic factor.
  • Quantitative liver fat can be obtained by 1H-MRS, but it is expensive and not recommended clinically.
  • Combining serum scores with transient elastography may improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce biopsy need.
  • Selected high-risk patients may be considered for repeat biopsy after at least 5 years.

sections.title: Natural history and complications
sections.contentHtml:
TransitionRate / pace in source
Simple steatosis → NASH F1–F212–40% over 8–13 years
NASH → F35–10%
NASH → cirrhosis F40–50% depending on population
Cirrhosis → HCC1–8% per year
NAFL fibrosis progression1 stage / 14 years
NASH fibrosis progression1 stage / 7 years
HypertensionDoubles fibrosis-progression rate
Major outcome

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in NAFLD, except when advanced fibrosis changes the balance. Cardiovascular screening is mandatory in the lecture.

  • NAFLD is an independent HCC risk factor even before cirrhosis, but systematic surveillance in non-cirrhotic NAFLD is not considered cost-effective.
  • Standard 6-monthly ultrasound ± AFP surveillance applies once cirrhosis is present.
  • Pediatric NASH-related cirrhosis has been reported as early as 8 years in the source.

sections.title: Lifestyle, pharmacotherapy and surgery
sections.contentHtml:
Foundation — every patientHealthy diet + habitual activity; 7–10% weight-loss target in overweight/obese NAFLD
Selected NASHOff-label pharmacotherapy, especially F2+ or high progression risk
Refractory obesity / advanced diseaseBariatric surgery or liver transplantation when indicated
Lifestyle componentTarget in source
Caloric restriction500–1,000 kcal/day deficit
Weight loss7–10% body weight
Activity150–200 min/week moderate intensity in 3–5 sessions; aerobic and resistance training
Diet qualityMediterranean pattern; reduce processed food and added fructose
AlcoholBelow 30 g/day in men and 20 g/day in women
CoffeeNo liver-related restriction
Pharmacotherapy status in the uploaded lecture

No drug is specifically approved for NAFLD/NASH. Pioglitazone or vitamin E may be used in selected NASH; metformin has little histological evidence. Statins may be used for LDL and cardiovascular risk but are not NASH therapy.

passages.title: 1.3 Multi-Organ Crosstalk in NAFLD
passages.text:
1.3 Multi-Organ Crosstalk in NAFLD
Organs Involved in NAFLD Pathogenesis (Inter-Organ Crosstalk)
› Adipose tissue: excess free fatty acids (FFAs) released → hepatic lipotoxicity and inflammation
› Pancreas: beta-cell dysfunction and insulin hypersecretion → hyperinsulinemia
› Gut (microbiome): dysbiosis → increased intestinal permeability → bacterial endotoxin → hepatic
TLR4 activation → inflammation
› Liver: central target — steatosis, necroinflammation, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis/HCC
› Lipids accumulating in the liver induce hepatic insulin resistance and inflammation — key driver of
NASH
1.4 Lipids induce hepatic IR and inflammation

02 Epidemiology & Prevalence
Screening · Incidence · Risk Groups
2.1 Prevalence & Burden
17–46% 7% 12–22% ~50%
Lean (normal-weight) Of chronic liver disease Diagnosed late — advanced
NAFLD in Western adults
individuals patients cirrhosis
• NAFLD parallels the prevalence of Metabolic Syndrome (MetS) and its components, which also
increase the risk of more advanced disease
• Prevalence is rising in parallel with global obesity and T2DM epidemics
• NAFLD is also found in 7% of lean (normal-weight) individuals — screening must not be based on
BMI alone
2.2 Screening Recommendations
Who to Screen (EASL Guidelines)
› Screen all patients with insulin resistance (IR) and/or metabolic risk factors (obesity, MetS) →
evaluate for NAFLD
› Screen all individuals with steatosis for secondary causes including careful alcohol intake
assessment
› Screen all NAFLD patients for coexisting chronic liver diseases that may worsen liver injury
› Screen all individuals with steatosis for MetS features, independent of liver enzyme levels
› In obesity / MetS: NAFLD screening should be part of routine work-up
Why Community Screening is Limited
› High direct and indirect costs
› Low predictive value of available non-invasive tests
› Risks associated with liver biopsy (required to confirm NASH)
› Lack of approved specific pharmacological treatments
→ BUT: Diagnosing NASH is valuable — it identifies patients at risk of fibrosis progression,
cirrhosis, and HCC

High fructose intake De novo lipogenesis in the liver; drives NASH progression
Sedentary behaviour Reduces peripheral glucose utilisation and muscle insulin sensitivity

passages.text:
3.4 Natural history of NAFLD over 8–13 years
NAFLD Natural History at 8–13 Years (Key Numbers)
Transition Rate
Simple steatosis → NASH (F1–F2 fibrosis) 12–40%
NASH → Advanced fibrosis (F3) 5–10%
NASH → Cirrhosis (F4) 0–50% (variable by population)
Cirrhosis → HCC 1–8% per year
Cirrhosis → Liver-related death / LTx ~13%
3.5 Liver Biopsy
• Liver biopsy is essential for the diagnosis of NASH
– Clinical, biochemical or imaging measures cannot distinguish NASH from steatosis
• NAFL encompasses
– Steatosis alone plus ONE of lobular or portal inflammation OR ballooning
• NASH requires
– Steatosis AND
– Lobular or portal inflammation AND
– Ballooning
• NAS scoring indicates disease severity
★ Recommendation: NASH must be diagnosed by liver biopsy showing steatosis +
hepatocyte ballooning + lobular inflammation. No non-invasive method can replace A 1
evidence rec. grade
this for diagnostic certainty

passages.title: 3.6 Role of non-invasive assessments
passages.text:
3.6 Role of non-invasive assessments
• Non-invasive markers should aim to:
– Identify the risk of NAFLD among individuals with increased metabolic risk in primary
care
– Identify those with a worse prognosis in secondary and tertiary care, E.g. severe NASH
– Monitor disease progression
– Predict response to therapeutic interventions
→ Achieving these aims could reduce the need for liver biopsy
3.7 Non-Invasive Assessment of Steatosis
• Steatosis should be documented whenever NAFLD is suspected
– Predicts future T2DM, cardiovascular events and arterial hypertension
– Quantification of fat content is of limited clinical relevance
• Except as a surrogate of treatment effectiveness
★ Recommendation: US is the preferred first-line diagnostic procedure for A 1
imaging of NAFLD, as it provides additional diagnostic information evidence rec. grade
Whenever imaging tools are not available or feasible serum biomarkers and scores
are an acceptable alternative for the diagnosis of steatosis
B 2
A quantitative estimation of liver fat can only be obtained by 1H-MRS. This technique
is of value in clinical trials and experimental studies, but is expensive and not A 1
recommended in the clinical setting
3.8 Non-Invasive Assessment of Fibrosis
Why Fibrosis Assessment Is the Priority
› Fibrosis stage is the MOST IMPORTANT prognostic factor in NAFLD
› Correlates directly with liver-related outcomes (decompensation, HCC) and all-cause mortality
› Advanced fibrosis indicates thorough investigation
★ Recommendation: Biomarkers, fibrosis scores, and transient elastography, are
acceptable non-invasive procedures to identify those at low risk of advanced A 2
evidence rec. grade
fibrosis/cirrhosis
Biomarkers/scores PLUS transient elastography might confer additional diagnostic
accuracy and reduce need for liver biopsy
B 2
Monitoring of fibrosis progression may rely on biomarkers/scores and transient
elastography, although this strategy requires validation
C 1
The identification of advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis by serum biomarkers/scores and/or
elastography is less accurate and needs to be confirmed by liver biopsy, according to B 2
the clinical context
In selected patients at high risk of liver disease progression, monitoring should include
C 2

3.10 Non-invasive assessment of paediatric NAFLD
• NAFLD should always be suspected in obese children
– Exclude other causes
– Evaluate elevated aminotransferase levels and liver hyperechogenicity
• Due to the poor sensitivity in overweight/obese children, non-invasive markers
and imaging techniques are the first diagnostic step

passages.title: 05 Diagnosis & Evaluation
passages.text:
05 Diagnosis & Evaluation
• Incidental discovery of steatosis indicates comprehensive evaluation
– Family and personal history of NAFLD-associated diseases
– Exclusion of secondary causes of steatosis
5.1 Initial Evaluation Protocol
Level Variable
Initial 1. Alcohol intake: <20 g/day (women), <30 g/day (men)
2. Personal and family history of diabetes, hypertension and CVD
3. BMI, waist circumference, change in body weight
4. Hepatitis B/hepatitis C virus infection
5. History of steatosis-associated drugs
6. Liver enzymes (ALT, AST, GGT)
7. Fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, OGTT, (fasting insulin [HOMA-IR])
8. Complete blood count
9. Serum total and HDL cholesterol, triacylglycerol, uric acid
10. Ultrasonography (if suspected for raised liver enzymes)
Extended 1. Ferritin and transferrin saturation
2. Tests for coeliac and thyroid diseases, polycystic ovary syndrome
3. Tests for rare liver diseases (Wilson, autoimmune disease, AATD)
5.2 Diagnostic Flowchart Summary
• Metabolic work-up must carefully assess all components of MetS
• Obesity/T2DM or raised liver enzymes in patients with metabolic risk factors should prompt non-
invasive screening to predict steatosis, NASH and fibrosis

passages.title: 06 Natural History & Complications
passages.text:
06 Natural History & Complications
Progression · CVD · HCC
• In general, NAFLD is a slowly progressive disease, both in adults and in children
6.1 Fibrosis Progression Rates
1 stage / 14 Cirrhosis age
1 stage / 7 yrs x2 faster ~20% of cases
yrs NASH Progression HTN: Doubles rate Rapid Progressors 8
NAFL Progression Paediatric NASH
★ Recommendation: NASH patients with fibrosis and hypertension should receive B 1
closer monitoring — arterial hypertension doubles the rate of fibrosis progression evidence rec. grade
• Pediatric NAFLD is of concern
– Potential for severe liver-related complications later in life
– NASH-related cirrhosis has been reported as early as 8 years of age
6.2 Cardiovascular Disease (CVD)
• Prevalence and incidence of CVD is HIGHER in NAFLD than in matched controls
→ Driven by the strong association between NAFLD and MetS components
• CVD is the leading cause of death in NAFLD — more common than liver-related death (except in
advanced fibrosis)
• CVD risk must be assessed in all NAFLD patients regardless of traditional risk factors
• CVD and metabolic risk factors are reported even in adolescents and children with NAFLD
★ Recommendation: Cardiovascular system screening is MANDATORY in all A 1
individuals with NAFLD — CV complications frequently dictate overall outcome evidence rec. grade

passages.title: 6.3 Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
passages.text:
6.3 Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
• NAFLD is a recognised independent risk factor for HCC, even in the pre-cirrhotic stage
• PNPLA3 rs738409 C>G gene polymorphism significantly increases HCC risk in NAFLD
• HCC surveillance in non-cirrhotic NAFLD is NOT yet considered cost-effective
• Large NAFLD population makes systematic HCC surveillance largely impracticable
Note on HCC Surveillance
› No formal recommendation on timing or cost-effectiveness of HCC surveillance in NAFLD can
currently be made
› Standard HCC surveillance (6-monthly USS ± AFP) applies to NAFLD patients who have reached
cirrhosis (F4)
› PNPLA3 polymorphism carriers may warrant enhanced surveillance — under study
07 Treatment
Lifestyle · Pharmacotherapy · Surgery · Liver Transplantation
• Epidemiology suggests a close relationship between an unhealthy lifestyle and NAFLD
7.1 Diet & Lifestyle Changes (Mandatory in ALL Patients)
Lifestyle is First-Line Treatment for Every Patient with NAFLD
› Modest weight loss reduces liver fat, improves hepatic IR, and produces NASH regression
› Weight loss of ≥7% body weight is associated with significant histological improvement
› A pragmatic, individually tailored approach: dietary restriction PLUS progressive aerobic
exercise/resistance training
› Patients without NASH or fibrosis: lifestyle counselling only — no pharmacotherapy
★ Recommendation: Structured programmes aimed at lifestyle changes towards C 2
healthy diet and habitual physical activity are advisable in NAFLD evidence rec. grade
Patients without NASH or fibrosis should receive counselling for healthy diet and
physical activity but no pharmacotherapy
B 2
In overweight/obese NAFLD, a 7–10% weight loss is the target of most lifestyle
interventions, and results in improvement of liver enzymes and histology
B 1

items: 3 Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
NAFLD is a recognised independent risk factor for HCC, even in the pre-cirrhotic stage
PNPLA3 rs738409 C>G gene polymorphism significantly increases HCC risk in NAFLD
HCC surveillance in non-cirrhotic NAFLD is NOT yet considered cost-effective
Large NAFLD population makes systematic HCC surveillance largely impracticable

7.2 Pharmacotherapy
Indications for Drug Treatment
› Progressive NASH
› Early-stage NASH with risk of fibrosis progression (age >50 yrs + T2DM + MetS + elevated ALT)
› Active NASH with high necroinflammatory activity
› Significant fibrosis: stage F2 and higher → preferred candidates
⚠ Critical Point — Current Pharmacotherapy Status
› NO drugs are specifically approved for NAFLD / NASH
› NO specific therapy can be formally recommended — all drug use is OFF-LABEL
› Treatment goal: reduce NASH-related mortality and prevent progression to cirrhosis or HCC
› Safety and tolerability are prerequisites given significant polypharmacy burden in these patients
★ Recommendation: Pharmacotherapy should be reserved for patients with
NASH, particularly for those with significant fibrosis (stage F2 and higher). Patients B 1
with less severe disease, but at high risk of disease progression could also be evidence rec. grade
candidates for treatment

passages.title: Available Agents and Evidence
passages.text:
Available Agents and Evidence
• Insulin sensitizers
– Little evidence of histological efficacy with metformin
– PPAR agonist pioglitazone better than placebo
• Improved all histological features except fibrosis
• Achieved resolution of NASH more often
• Antioxidants
– Vitamin E may improve steatosis, inflammation and ballooning and resolve NASH in
some patients
• Concerns about long-term safety exist
★ Recommendation: While no firm recommendations can be made, pioglitazone* or B 2
vitamin E† or their combination could be used for NASH evidence rec. grade
The optimal duration of therapy is unknown; in patients with increased ALT at
baseline, treatment should be stopped if there is no reduction in aminotransferases C 2
after 6 months of therapy
• Lipid-lowering agents
– Statins have not been adequately tested in NASH
★ Recommendation: Statins may be confidently used to reduce LDL cholesterol and
prevent cardiovascular risk, with no benefits or harm to liver disease. B 1
Similarly, n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reduce both plasma and liver lipids, but evidence rec. grade
there are no data to support their use specifically for NASH
MOA of pharmacological treatments for NAFLD

passages.title: Paediatric NAFLD
passages.text:
Paediatric NAFLD
• Diet and exercise training reduce steatosis, but do not affect ballooning, inflammation,
and fibrosis
• The long-term outcome of paediatric NASH remains poor
– Drugs have shown beneficial effects but fibrotic lesions are refractory to treatment
★ Recommendation: Diet and physical activity improve steatosis and hepatic
inflammation in paediatric NAFLD, but no beneficial effects on fibrosis have ever been B 1
demonstrated. No safe drug treatment has proven effective on fibrosis in evidence rec. grade
paediatric NAFLD
7.3 Surgical Treatment
A. Bariatric Surgery
• Indicated in patients UNRESPONSIVE to lifestyle changes and pharmacotherapy
• Significantly reduces weight and metabolic complications
• Prospective data show improvement in ALL histological lesions of NASH, including fibrosis
• Results are stable in the long term
★ Recommendation: Bariatric surgery reduces liver fat and likely reduces NASH
progression. Prospective data show improvement in all NASH histological lesions B 1
evidence rec. grade
including fibrosis
B. Liver Transplantation (LTx)
★ Recommendation: LTx is an accepted procedure in patients with NASH and end-
stage liver disease. Overall survival is comparable to other indications, despite a A 1
higher cardiovascular mortality. Patients with NASH and liver failure and/or HCC evidence rec. grade
are candidates for liver transplantation
